title: Who am I?
hook: Ramana Maharshi taught self-enquiry: ask "who am I?" and trace the "I" to its source

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan: one voice calls, the room answers, singing the names. Your line was call and response. In a conversation, did you give back what you heard before adding your own? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

A clinic intake form asks who you are, in pieces. Name. Address. Occupation. Emergency contact. Allergies. Each box is small, and each answer is true. Fill them all in and you've described a person well enough to be treated, billed and called back. In South India, at the foot of a hill called Arunachala, a quiet teacher named Ramana Maharshi asked the same question with no boxes at all. And he didn't want it filled in. He wanted it followed, the way you'd follow a stream uphill to see where it starts. Today's word is his question: who am I?
screen: `AN INTAKE FORM, IN PIECES.` → `A HILL CALLED ARUNACHALA.` → `FOLLOWED, NOT FILLED IN.`

segments.voice: Ramana's teaching survives in short works and in conversations his visitors wrote down. One small booklet carries the question as its title: in Tamil, Nan Yar, who am I? This is a paraphrase, not his words, but the method goes like this. Notice that every thought you have is somebody's thought. Before the worry, before the plan, there is an I that has it. In Ramana's account, that sense of I is the first thought, and every other thought rises after it. So when a thought comes, don't follow it out into the world. Turn it around. Ask: to whom did this come? The answer comes back: to me. Then ask: and who am I? Not as a riddle to solve with words. Ramana goes through the obvious answers: not the body, not the senses, not even the thinking mind. One way readers put it: each of these can be noticed, and the I is the one noticing. The point is to keep attention on the I itself, and trace it back toward where it rises. He gives a striking picture for what the question does. At a cremation, someone stirs the fire with a stick, keeping it burning. At the end, the stick goes into the fire too. The question who am I, he says, works on all the other thoughts like that stick, and in the end it burns up as well. Then the asking stops, and what remains is not another thought. So this is a question that isn't meant to end in an answer. Yesterday was loud, a room singing names. Today is a single word, I, held up to the light and followed home.
screen: `EVERY THOUGHT IS SOMEBODY'S.` · `TO WHOM DID THIS COME?` · `NOT THE BODY, NOT THE MIND.` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask "who am I?" three times. Settle, and let the breath slow. Ask it once, inside, slowly. Then wait. Don't answer with a word. If an answer shows up anyway, a job, a name, a mood, notice it, and ask: to whom did this come? Then ask again: who am I? Wait longer this time. And a third time, with the longest silence of all. You're not looking for a reply. You're looking at where the question lands. The bell holds the time.
Who am I? Ramana Maharshi's self-enquiry: meet each thought by asking to whom it came, and follow the I back to its source. Today's word.
Your line: who am I. Today, when a strong thought grabs you, irritation, pride, worry, pause and ask to whom it came, and watch it loosen for a moment. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-enquiry by meeting each thought with the question "to whom did this come?" and turning attention back to the sense of I, in sitting practice and through the day.

fork.setup: in the middle of your sit, a thought shows up: I'm bad at this. what does Ramana's method do?
options: argue with it until it goes away.
follow it to see where it leads.
ask: to whom did this come?
fork.reveal: to me. and who am I? the thought isn't fought or followed. attention turns back toward the I that had it.

what a scholar hears: Nan Yar, in Tamil. Ramana calls the I-thought the first thought, sets aside body, senses and mind, and compares the question to a stick that stirs a pyre and burns at the end.

notes: Ramana Maharshi is a modern teacher: paraphrased only, never quoted, and the script says so ('this is a paraphrase, not his words').
